benchComp.name: Competition bench press
how: Eyes under the bar. Feet planted. Moderate arch from the UPPER back, never the lower.
Grip: RING FINGER ON THE RINGS — about 73 cm, and about 8 cm inside the legal maximum. This never changes on the competition lift.
Shoulder blades back and DOWN — think about putting them in your back pockets.
Unrack, then pause 2–3 s to re-settle the arch, re-plant the feet, re-tighten the lats.
Lower for ~2 seconds to the same spot every rep, just below the nipple line.
Pause ~1 s on the chest, bar dead, still tight.
Drive with maximal intent. Bar path is a J-curve: back and up, then vertical.
benchComp.why: The lift everything else serves. It is a skill as much as a strength quality, which is why it never rotates out.
subs: Nothing. This one is the point.
benchComp.watch: Your competition grip is fixed. Grip variation belongs in the variation slot, not on the lift you are measuring — the whole progression depends on holding one thing steady. Rushing the eccentric is your single biggest technical leak. It makes the touch point inconsistent and adds a bounce that inflates numbers without building the strength underneath.

benchVar.name: Bench variation (retired — split by variation)
how: Close-grip: hands ~1.5 shoulder widths, elbows tucked ~45°.
Spoto: stop 2–3 cm above the chest, hold 1 s, press. No bounce, no contact.
Pin press: bar starts dead on pins 5–10 cm off the chest. No eccentric at all.
benchVar.why: Supplemental pressing strength through a different stimulus, and it spreads joint load across grips and ranges. Rotates every block, never weekly. Split into one exercise per variation so each carries its own percentage of the competition max; kept so sets logged before the split keep their name.
benchVar.watch: Do not copy equipped lifters and load up board presses and rack lockouts. You are raw with long arms — you fail off the chest, not at lockout.

benchSpeed.name: Speed bench
how: 65–75% of your max. Six sets of three.
Controlled ~2 s down, then accelerate as hard as you physically can.
Rest 90–120 s. If the bar is not visibly faster than your volume sets, the load is wrong.
benchSpeed.why: A fourth bench exposure that costs almost nothing — non-failure work at this effort recovers in about six hours. It is skill practice plus the intent effect, not a growth stimulus.
subs: Same lift, lighter. There is no substitute for the competition movement here.
benchSpeed.watch: Counts as ZERO hypertrophy volume. Sets at RPE 5–6 are motor-pattern practice. Counting them would inflate your ledger and tempt you to make this day hard — which is the most common way people wreck a heavy/light structure.

inclineDB.name: Incline dumbbell press (30°)
how: Bench at 30°, not 45°. Above ~45° this quietly becomes a shoulder press.
Same scapular setup as flat bench.
Full stretch at the bottom — that is where the growth is.
Do not lock out hard; keep tension on the pec.
inclineDB.why: Your main upper-chest driver, and upper chest is a named aesthetic priority. Dumbbells give a longer stretch; used in accumulation blocks.
inclineDB.watch: Dumbbells in accumulation blocks, Smith in intensification blocks. One per block — not alternating weekly.

inclineSmith.name: Incline Smith press (30°)
how: Bench at 30°, not 45°. Above ~45° this quietly becomes a shoulder press.
Same scapular setup as flat bench — blades back and DOWN.
The fixed bar path lets you load heavier and progress in smaller steps than dumbbells.
Full stretch at the bottom, no hard lockout at the top.
inclineSmith.why: Your second upper-chest driver, run alongside the dumbbell version rather than instead of it. The Smith loads heavier and progresses in 1.25 kg steps, which dumbbells cannot; the dumbbells give the longer stretch. Running one in each session gives you both mechanisms every week and two clean progression lines.
inclineSmith.watch: This is the precision-loading slot. Add 1.25–2.5 kg when all sets hit the top of the range — do not chase it with sloppy reps.

inclineFly.name: Incline cable fly
how: Slight elbow bend, fixed throughout the rep.
Let the arms travel BEHIND the torso at the bottom.
Think about the stretch, not the squeeze.
inclineFly.why: Upper chest in the fully lengthened position, which is where the evidence for growth is strongest — and it does it with almost no joint or systemic cost.
subs: Pec deck with the seat raised
inclineFly.watch: Goes to failure every set. This is exactly the kind of exercise failure is for.

cableFly.name: Cable fly / pec deck (flat)
how: Handles at chest height, slight elbow bend held fixed.
Let the arms travel behind the torso at the bottom — the stretch is the point.
Squeeze without shrugging. Slow eccentric.
cableFly.why: Added so that no session in the rotation contributes zero hypertrophy. A machine or cable fly is close to free systemically, which means it can sit on the speed day without compromising what that day is for.
cableFly.watch: Every set to failure. This is exactly the sort of exercise failure exists for.

dip.name: Weighted dip
how: Slight forward lean for chest bias; upright for triceps.
STOP the descent when your upper arm is parallel to the floor.
Control the negative.
dip.why: Loaded pressing through a different plane, plus real triceps work. One of your named priority lifts.
dip.watch: Going deeper than parallel is where shoulders get hurt for no extra benefit. Long arms make this worse, not better.

pullupNorm.name: Weighted pull-up — normal grip
how: Pronated, hands roughly shoulder-width to a little outside.
Dead hang start, shoulders depressed before you pull.
Drive the elbows down and back. Chest toward the bar.
Control the descent — this is where most of the growth is.
pullupNorm.why: Your tracked vertical pull and the balanced version of the movement. Fixed for the whole block so the progression line stays clean.
pullupNorm.watch: This is the one that carries your progression. The other two grips are their own exercises with their own numbers — do not compare them to each other.

chinup.name: Weighted chin-up — supinated
how: Supinated, roughly shoulder width.
Full dead hang — at the bottom, the shoulder is flexed and the biceps long head is stretched.
Control the descent.
chinup.why: Your strongest grip, and the only vertical pull that meaningfully trains the biceps. At the bottom of a dead hang the long head is loaded in a lengthened position, which is exactly where it grows.
chinup.watch: Chin-ups get limited by your biceps before your back, which is why this is a separate exercise rather than the tracked one.

pulldown.name: Lat pulldown (wide)
how: Slight backward lean, chest up.
Pull to the upper chest, elbows down and back.
Full stretch at the top — let the shoulder blade rise.
pulldown.why: Lat volume that is easier to load precisely than pull-ups, on a day where you are already fatigued from bench volume.

rowCSR.name: Chest-supported / cable row
how: Chest up, no torso swing.
Pull to the lower ribs.
Let the shoulder blade protract fully at the front for the stretch.
rowCSR.why: Heavy upper-back work is the strongest cross-coach consensus point for a big bench — it builds the pressing platform, recovers fast, and protects the shoulder under high pressing frequency. Effectively free volume.
rowCSR.watch: Vary the ANGLE between sessions — one higher toward the upper chest, one lower toward the ribs — rather than swapping machines.

facepull.name: Face pull
how: Rope at roughly eye height.
Pull toward the face, elbows high, and externally rotate at the end.
High reps, controlled.
facepull.why: Rear delts plus shoulder health. Added because you press four times a week and rear delt frequency was the weakest link in the original draft.

reardelt.name: Rear delt fly
how: Slight forward lean, elbows soft and fixed.
Lead with the elbows, not the hands.
High reps, to failure.
reardelt.why: Direct rear delt. Aesthetically it is what makes shoulders look three-dimensional from the side, and it counterbalances heavy pressing.

lateral.name: Cable lateral raise
how: Run the cable BEHIND your body so there is tension in the stretched position.
Lead with the elbow. Slight forward lean.
Stop at shoulder height — above that the traps take over.
Slow negative.
lateral.why: Your highest-priority aesthetic muscle. Hit in five of six sessions because side delts recover fast and the per-session ceiling is low.
lateral.watch: Cable and dumbbell versions were found equivalent in a 2025 within-participant study. Use whichever lets you reach genuine failure without swinging — but behind-the-body cable is the upgrade.

ohpLadder.name: Overhead press ladder
how: Rung 1: seated neutral-grip dumbbell press.
Rung 2: landmine press. Rung 3: high-incline (60°).
Rung 4: seated barbell. Rung 5: standing barbell.
Four weeks minimum per rung. Advance only if the previous rung was completely symptom-free.
ohpLadder.why: Rebuilding the overhead position rather than just adding the lift back. Your shoulder pain came at the very start of your training on a lift you have not touched since — that is a preparedness problem, not a structural one.
subs: Drop back a rung. That IS the substitute.
ohpLadder.watch: Drop a rung at the first sign of dull ache. No exceptions. You have 33 weeks; there is no rush. Watch for lumbar hyperextension as you climb — that is your back compensating for shoulder range you do not have yet.

triOH.name: Overhead cable/rope extension
how: Elbows in and pointed up.
Full stretch behind the head — that is the whole point.
Squeeze at lockout without flaring the elbows.
triOH.why: Bench pressing barely loads the triceps LONG head, because it is biarticular and shoulder position during pressing creates conflicting length demands. This is one of only two movements in the plan that actually trains it.
triOH.watch: The long head is the biggest of the three triceps heads and the main driver of arm size from the back. It was under-served in the first draft — this is the fix.

skull.name: EZ-bar skullcrusher
how: Lower to the forehead or just behind the head.
Keep the upper arm angled back slightly — pure vertical removes the long-head stretch.
Controlled negative; this is where the tension is.
skull.why: Second long-head exposure of the week, on a day with no pressing so it costs your bench nothing.
skull.watch: If your elbows complain, switch to the cable overhead version — same head, gentler joint.

pushdown.name: Cable pushdown
how: Elbows pinned to your sides. No shoulder movement.
Squeeze hard at the bottom.
pushdown.why: Lateral and medial head volume at essentially zero systemic cost.

curlIncline.name: Incline dumbbell curl
how: Bench at ~45°, arms hanging BEHIND the torso.
That behind-the-body position is the long-head stretch — it is the entire reason to use an incline.
Full extension at the bottom every rep.
curlIncline.why: The biceps long head is the outer head — it is what creates the peak, and it only grows properly when trained in the stretched position.

curlBayesian.name: Bayesian cable curl
how: Stand a step in front of a low cable, arm trailing behind you.
Keep the elbow behind the torso for the whole rep.
Slow eccentric all the way to full extension.
curlBayesian.why: Second long-head exposure. Cable tension in the stretched position is more consistent than a dumbbell here.
curlBayesian.watch: Added in the audit — the long head was only being trained once a week in the first draft.

curlEZ.name: EZ-bar or preacher curl
how: Preacher pad or strict standing.
Full range. No swinging, no hip drive.
Squeeze at the top.
curlEZ.why: Short head — the inner head, which adds width to the arm when viewed from the front.

curlHammer.name: Hammer or reverse curl
how: Neutral grip (hammer) or pronated (reverse).
No swing. Controlled both directions.
curlHammer.why: Brachialis and forearm. Brachialis sits under the biceps and pushes it up — growing it makes the arm look bigger from every angle.

wrist.name: Wrist curl + reverse wrist curl
how: Forearms braced on a bench or your thighs.
Full range, high reps.
Always to failure.
wrist.why: Dual purpose: forearms are on your aesthetic list, AND wrist/forearm work protects your elbows from the high pressing frequency. One of very few things in the plan with no trade-off.

cableCrunch.name: Kneeling cable crunch
how: Kneel facing away from a high cable, rope behind your head.
Flex the SPINE, not the hips — the movement is curling your ribs toward your pelvis.
Keep the hips fixed. If your hips are moving, it has become a hip-flexor exercise.
Slow, controlled, squeeze hard at the bottom.
cableCrunch.why: The best loaded movement for rectus abdominis hypertrophy. Abs respond to progressive load like any other muscle — the reason most people have untrained abs is that they only ever do bodyweight reps.
cableCrunch.watch: Controlled flexion against a cable is fine for your back. Ballistic sit-ups with a loaded spine are not — that is repeated end-range lumbar flexion under load, which is the pattern most likely to aggravate a disc-related issue.

hangingRaise.name: Hanging leg raise
how: Dead hang, shoulders active (not fully relaxed).
Raise the knees and then TILT THE PELVIS BACK at the top — that posterior tilt is what actually loads the abs.
No swinging. Lower under control.
Progress by straightening the legs, then by holding a dumbbell between the feet.
hangingRaise.why: Trains the rectus from the bottom up, which the crunch pattern does less well, and doubles as grip work.
hangingRaise.watch: If you only lift the knees without tilting the pelvis, this is a hip-flexor exercise and your abs are barely working. The tilt is the rep.

abWheel.name: Ab wheel rollout
how: From the knees to start. Ribs down, glutes squeezed, pelvis tucked.
Roll out only as far as you can WITHOUT the lower back arching.
That range will be short at first. Short and honest beats long and sagging.
abWheel.why: Anti-extension — the abs work to stop the spine extending rather than to flex it. It builds exactly the bracing strength that protects your lower back and stabilises you under a heavy bench.
abWheel.watch: The moment your lower back arches, the load transfers straight to your lumbar spine. Given your back, stop the range well before that point and add range over months, not weeks.

pallof.name: Pallof press
how: Stand side-on to a cable at chest height.
Press straight out and resist the rotation. Nothing should twist.
Hold 2–3 s at full extension. Breathe.
pallof.why: Anti-rotation. Obliques and deep core, trained isometrically without any spinal loading at all — the safest core work available to you.
pallof.watch: Zero risk to your back. If anything ever aggravates, this is the one to keep.

legpress.name: Leg press — feet low and narrow
how: Feet low and mid-width on the platform. This is the quad-biased, heavier one.
STOP the descent the moment your pelvis starts to tuck.
Control the descent. Do not lock the knees hard at the top.
legpress.why: Your main quad driver without any spinal loading. Session B's version: heavier, moderate depth, feet low.
legpress.watch: That pelvic tuck at the bottom is loaded lumbar flexion — the exact thing that irritates your back. A slightly shorter range with a neutral spine beats a deep rep that costs you a week.

hackBulg.name: Hack squat or Bulgarian split squat
how: Hack squat: control the descent, knees track over toes.
Bulgarian: rear foot elevated, torso slightly forward, most of the load through the front leg.
hackBulg.why: A second quad pattern, chosen by whichever your back tolerates on the day.
subs: Leg press — feet low and narrow
hackBulg.watch: Bulgarians are back-friendlier than most loaded squat patterns because the load is lighter and the spine stays more vertical.

legcurlSeat.name: Seated leg curl
how: Seated beats lying — hip flexion puts the hamstring at a longer length.
Control the return; do not let the weight snap back.
legcurlSeat.why: Hamstrings, at a long muscle length, with zero spinal load. Given you are not deadlifting, this is your main posterior chain work.

legcurlLie.name: Lying leg curl or Nordic
how: Hips down on the pad, no hip lift to cheat the rep.
Nordic: control the descent as far as you can, push back up.
legcurlLie.why: Second hamstring exposure. Different hip angle to the seated version.

quadext.name: Quad extension
how: Pause at full extension.
Slow negative.
High reps, to failure.
quadext.why: The rectus femoris crosses the hip, so it is under-trained by pressing movements where the hip also extends. This picks it up.

calfStand.name: Standing calf raise
how: 2-second pause at full stretch at the bottom.
Full range. Do not bounce.
calfStand.watch: Rushing calf work is the main reason calves do not grow. The stretch pause is not optional.

calfSeat.name: Seated calf raise
how: 2-second pause at the bottom, same as standing.
Higher reps than standing.
calfSeat.why: Seated (knee bent) targets the soleus, which the standing version largely misses.

revhyper.name: Reverse hyperextension
how: Controlled, no swinging.
Stop at neutral — do not hyperextend.
revhyper.why: A decompression and blood-flow exercise for your lower back, not a strength lift. You already do these and they stay in.
revhyper.watch: If it ever aggravates rather than relieves, stop and tell me. That is diagnostic information.

jumps.name: Box jumps / broad jumps
how: Always first in the session, always fresh.
Land quietly — noise means you are absorbing force badly.
STEP DOWN from the box. Never jump down.
Full recovery between sets, 2–3 min.
jumps.why: Vertical jump comes from rate of force development and reactive ability, which heavy machine work does not train. Plyometrics are the direct transfer.
jumps.watch: Low volume, high quality. Twelve good jumps beat thirty mediocre ones. Stop the moment reps get less crisp. If your back objects at all, these come out and we revisit. Introduced week 7, not before.

staticHold.name: Static hold (rack pins)
how: Rack pins set, spotter present, always. No exceptions.
2–3 holds of 5–10 seconds at 105–115% of your current max.
Unrack, hold at lockout, re-rack. Do not lower the bar.
Full recovery between holds — this is a load exposure, not conditioning.
staticHold.why: Desensitises you to supramaximal load, builds lockout and connective-tissue tolerance, and can potentiate the sets that follow. You reported these coincided with your strongest bench, and that is consistent with what they do: they make competition weight feel light.
subs: Pin press 5–10 cm off the chest
staticHold.watch: Introduced at block 2, never before — hanging 115% of your max on your elbows before the connective tissue has re-adapted is how you buy a six-week layoff. Counts as ZERO hypertrophy volume: a 7-second hold is a neural and connective exposure, not a growth stimulus.

hipThrust.name: Hip thrust (barbell or machine)
how: Upper back on the bench, chin tucked, ribs down.
Drive through the heels and finish with the hips, not the lower back.
Pause a beat at lockout. Do not hyperextend.
hipThrust.why: The largest muscular omission in v1. Direct hip extension with almost no spinal load, placed in B where it cannot interfere with a bench day.
hipThrust.watch: Your back history means the finish position matters more than the load. Stop the rep at neutral.

rowOneArm.name: One-arm lat-biased cable row
how: Elbow tucked close to the body, drive it back and down.
Let the shoulder blade reach fully forward at the front for the stretch.
No torso rotation to finish the rep.
rowOneArm.why: A lat-biased pull to complement the upper-back-biased row in A. One arm at a time gives a longer range and a fuller stretch than a bar.

rowMachine.name: Stable machine / chest-supported row
how: Chest against the pad, no torso swing.
Pull to the lower ribs, squeeze without shrugging.
Control the return; let the blade protract at the front.
rowMachine.why: The cheapest possible pulling exposure, in F, where anything fatiguing would compromise the heavy bench the next day.

reardeltPecDeck.name: Reverse pec-deck rear-delt fly
how: Slight elbow bend held fixed. Lead with the elbows, not the hands.
Stop when the upper arms reach the torso line.
Slow the return.
reardeltPecDeck.why: A machine keeps the rear delt loaded through the whole range without the stabilisation cost of a free-weight fly.

reardeltCable.name: Cable rear-delt fly
how: Cross the cables in front, lead with the elbows.
Constant tension — do not let the stack touch down.
Stop at the torso line.
reardeltCable.why: Cable tension is most even in the stretched position, which is where the rear delt is hardest to load.

curlHighCable.name: High-cable / stable machine curl
how: Upper arm slightly forward of the torso.
Squeeze at the top without swinging the elbow.
Full extension at the bottom, controlled.
curlHighCable.why: A short-head-biased curl pattern. Biceps work across the rotation deliberately covers lengthened, preacher, Bayesian, hammer and high-cable positions rather than repeating one curl.

curlReverse.name: Reverse cable / EZ curl
how: Pronated grip, wrists neutral and locked.
Elbows pinned to the sides.
Do not swing to start the rep.
curlReverse.why: Brachioradialis and wrist extensors — the part of the forearm ordinary curling and gripping does not train.

wristRoller.name: Wrist roller / flexion-extension superset
how: Arms out in front, roll up and lower under control both directions.
Or superset supported wrist flexion straight into extension.
Always to genuine failure.
wristRoller.why: Broadened forearm coverage: flexion, extension, brachioradialis and rotation now appear across all six sessions rather than repeating generic wrist curls.

cableRotation.name: Cable pronation / supination (retired)
how: Elbow at the side, fixed. Rotate the forearm only.
Full controlled range in both directions.
Light load; this is a rotation drill, not a curl.
cableRotation.why: The rotational component of forearm training, absent from v1. Cheap, and it complements flexion and extension work. Split into two exercises so each direction is tracked separately; kept here so sets logged before the split keep their name.

wristFlex.name: Supported wrist flexion
how: Forearms braced on a bench, palms up.
Full range, high reps, to failure.
No elbow movement.
wristFlex.why: Wrist flexors, trained directly and separately from the extensors so both actually get a dose.

wristExt.name: Supported wrist extension
how: Forearms braced, palms down.
Light load, full range, to failure.
Control the lowering.
wristExt.why: Wrist extensors — the side that ordinary gripping never trains, and the side implicated in elbow pain.

cablePronation.name: Cable pronation
how: Elbow pinned to your side and fixed — the forearm is the only thing that moves.
Start palm-up, rotate to palm-down against the cable, and control the way back.
Light. This is a rotation drill, not a curl.
cablePronation.why: The pronating half of the forearm rotation work, separated so each direction is loaded and progressed on its own.

cableSupination.name: Cable supination
how: Elbow pinned to your side and fixed — the forearm is the only thing that moves.
Start palm-down, rotate to palm-up against the cable, and control the way back.
Light. This is a rotation drill, not a curl.
cableSupination.why: The supinating half of the forearm rotation work. Supination is also the biceps’ second job, so this doubles as direct biceps work at a short length.

legpressGlute.name: Leg press — feet high and wide, deep
how: Feet high and wide on the platform, toes turned slightly out.
Three seconds down, as deep as your pelvis allows. No bounce at the bottom.
STOP the descent the moment your pelvis starts to tuck.
Much lighter than session B — the range is the point, not the load.
legpressGlute.why: The long-length, slow, glute-and-adductor half of your leg pressing. Same machine as session B, a different exercise: high and wide shortens knee travel and lengthens hip travel, so the glutes and adductors do the work the quads do in B.
subs: Leg press, feet high, at whatever depth is clean
legpressGlute.watch: That pelvic tuck at the bottom is loaded lumbar flexion — the exact thing that irritates your back. A slightly shorter range with a neutral spine beats a deep rep that costs you a week.

backExt45.name: 45° back extension
how: Pads at the crease of the hip, not on the thighs.
Back flat. Hinge purely at the hip, and feel it entirely in the hamstrings.
STOP when your torso is in line with your legs. Never above it.
Hug a plate to the chest only once fifteen clean bodyweight reps are easy.
backExt45.why: The hamstrings do two jobs — bending the knee and extending the hip — and the plan only ever trained the first. This is the hip-extension half, and it loads the glutes at a long length where the hip thrust loads them short.
subs: Romanian deadlift, only if your back allows it
backExt45.watch: Coming up past the line of your legs is lumbar extension under load — the mirror image of the pelvic tuck at the bottom of a leg press. Stop at the line.

benchClose.name: Close-grip bench press
how: Hands about shoulder width — index fingers just inside the smooth rings.
Elbows tucked a little more than competition. Wrists stacked over the elbows.
Paused, one second, like the competition lift.
benchClose.why: The single best bench assistance exercise: same groove, more triceps, and it trains the transition zone where your press stalls.
subs: Bench with a slightly narrower grip than competition
benchClose.watch: Do not go so narrow that your wrists hurt. Shoulder width is close grip; touching plates is a wrist exercise.

benchPause.name: Long-pause bench press — 3 s
how: Competition grip and setup.
Touch, then hold motionless for a full three seconds.
Stay tight through the pause — it is not a rest. Then press hard.
benchPause.why: Removes the stretch reflex entirely, so the press starts from a dead position. Builds force off the chest and kills a bounce habit.
benchPause.watch: A pause is not a rest. If you go loose under the bar the shoulder takes it.

benchPin.name: Pin press — bar set just below the sticking point
how: Set the pins so the bar starts with your upper arm JUST BELOW horizontal — about 2 cm under where you stall.
Bar rests dead on the pins between reps. Stay tight; do not relax under it.
Press through the sticking point, not from above it.
benchPin.why: The most specific attack on a transition-zone sticking point: you start dead at the height where you stop, with zero elastic contribution.
benchPin.watch: Set too high and it becomes a board press and trains the lockout instead, which is not your weak point. Set it BELOW the stall.

benchWide.name: Wide-grip bench press
how: A thumb-length wider than competition, no more.
Paused, one second.
Shorter range off the chest; the lockout is the hard part.
benchWide.why: Shortens the range and shifts work toward the pecs. A different reading on the same lift, once the weak point is addressed.
benchWide.watch: Very wide grips are a shoulder risk for no extra benefit. One thumb-length wider is enough.

benchFeetUp.name: Feet-up bench press
how: Feet on the bench or in the air. No leg drive at all.
Competition grip, paused.
Brace hard — the only thing holding position is your trunk.
benchFeetUp.why: Removes leg drive, so it measures upper-body pressing on its own. Also exposes whether your arch is doing the work your chest should.
benchFeetUp.watch: Less stable. Drop the load and get a spotter.

sessions.name: Heavy bench, upper chest, back and triceps
sessions.purpose: The session that makes competition weight feel ordinary. A heavy top single finds the day's load; the back-offs are what actually build it.
sessions.key: A single alone was worth +11.4 kg in six weeks with a 6% chance of being real. Single plus back-offs was +33.7 kg with a 99.6% chance. The single is a load-finder; the back-offs are the training.

slots.note: Optional experiment. Primer before the top work, or training hold after all bench work — never both.

slots.effort: 1–2 RIR; final set may reach failure in high mode
1–2 RIR
Elbows 45–60°; final set RPE 9
2 RIR, 1 RIR, technical failure

sessions.name: Lower body, glutes, biceps, core and side delts
sessions.purpose: A true separator between hard pressing days. Everything here is a machine or a cable, so failure costs the rep and nothing else.
sessions.key: There is no direct chest or triceps work in this session, and that is the point — it exists so the bench sessions either side of it can be hard.

slots.effort: Heavy and quad-biased. Feet low, depth stops at the pelvic tuck.
The heavy hip thrust of the week. Ribs down, finish with the glutes.
Knee flexion. Session D takes the hip-extension half.

sessions.name: AMRAP, bench variation, chest and triceps
sessions.purpose: The measurement session. The AMRAP goes first, fresh, and a non-pressing day follows it.
sessions.key: A tired reading is a corrupted reading. Standardisation beats heroics: same pause, same grip, same order, every time.

slots.effort: 1–2 RIR; no failure
2 RIR, 1 RIR, technical failure
Final set RPE 9
First two 1–2 RIR; final RPE 9 to protect elbows

sessions.name: Lower body, back, biceps, rear/side delts and core
sessions.purpose: The second separator. Jumps first because power work is worthless when tired, then pulling, arms and the rest of the leg dose.
sessions.key: Two sets on the second leg press are deliberate: it is secondary work after the hack squat, not the session's primary lift.

slots.effort: Crisp reps; stop at any loss of height
Done fresh, second in the session.
Three seconds down, feet high and wide, full clean depth. Light.
Lighter than B. Pause a full second at lockout.
Hamstring-biased. Stop at the line of your legs.
Higher reps than session B. Finish the quads off.
Curl the hips up at the top, not just legs to 90°.

sessions.name: Bench volume, incline Smith and chest/triceps
sessions.purpose: The hardest hypertrophy-specific bench work of the rotation, with a separator before it and only the cheap F after it.
sessions.key: The Smith index set sits after the competition-bench work on purpose: it protects the priority lift while keeping an objective 80×8-becomes-85×8 progress anchor.

slots.note: Index set to technical failure, then two back-offs after an 8–12% load reduction.

slots.label: back-offs
slots.effort: 1–2 RIR
Full overhead stretch; final set RPE 9, RPE 10 in high mode
2 RIR, 1 RIR, technical failure
Controlled

knowledge.t: The three rules everything rests on
knowledge.c:
1 · Buy strength and size separately. Strength comes from heavy work at low volume. Size comes from submaximal work at high volume. Trying to buy both from the same sets is exactly what maxing every session was — and the bench is the most volume-dependent of the three big lifts, so it punished that approach hardest.

2 · Fatigue tracks how close you go to failure, not how many sets you do. Six sets at 3 reps in reserve recover as fast as three sets at 3 RIR. Three sets to failure cost 24–48 hours. That single finding is what makes benching four times a week possible.

3 · Failure is aimed, not cut. It goes on cables, machines and isolation, where it is the actual mechanism of growth and costs almost nothing systemically. It never goes on heavy pressing, where the strength data says it buys nothing at all.

knowledge.t: How long each session should take
knowledge.c:
These assume you actually take the prescribed rest periods. If you are finishing much faster, you are rushing; much slower, you are on your phone.

  • A · Heavy bench + back — 27 sets, 85–95 min. The longest, because heavy singles need 3–5 min between attempts.
  • B · Lower + arms — 28 sets, 75–85 min. Dense; most of it is 60–90 s rests.
  • C · AMRAP + bench variation — 27 sets, 70–80 min. The AMRAP is a measurement, so it goes first, straight after the ramp.
  • D · Lower + delts + jumps — 33 sets, 95–105 min. Four of those sets are jumps with full recovery.
  • E · Bench volume + incline Smith — 32 sets, 70–80 min. Two of those are the forearm rotation split into its two directions — the same work as before, counted as two exercises instead of one, so the minutes did not move.
  • F · Speed bench + overhead + back — 23 sets, 75–85 min. Most exercises, but six of those sets are cheap speed work.

Add 8–10 minutes of warm-up to each. These grew when we added the core work and the extra arm and chest volume — you said length was not a problem, so I took you at your word. If a session is consistently overrunning, tell me and I will trim it rather than have you skip the last exercises, which are always the isolation work you actually want.

knowledge.t: The five biggest mistakes, in order of cost
knowledge.c:
1 · Letting the heavy single creep into a max. This is the one that already cost you a year. RPE 8 becomes 8.5 becomes 9.5 becomes a max, and it happens over weeks so you never notice the moment. The defence is mechanical, not motivational: write the load range down before the session, cap it at two singles above 90%, never miss a rep. If you had to psych up, it was too heavy.

2 · Skipping the back-off sets. A heavy single alone was worth +11.4 kg over six weeks with a 6% probability of being a real change. The same single plus back-off triples was +33.7 kg with a 99.6% probability. The single is a load-finder. Skipping the back-offs recreates precisely the failure mode in your history.

3 · Making the speed day hard. Session D only works because it is cheap. The moment it becomes another heavy day, you have four hard bench sessions a week and the structure collapses. If the bar is not visibly faster than your volume sets, the load is wrong.

4 · Rushing the eccentric. Your specific technical leak. It makes the touch point inconsistent, the bar path variable, and adds a bounce that inflates your numbers without building the strength underneath. Two seconds down, every rep.

5 · Chasing the number in month six. If you are at a normal-day 132 kg in February, the correct move is to keep building — not to start maxing to prove something. The plan does not end in March; the deadline is self-imposed.

knowledge.t: Week 1 — the testing protocol
knowledge.c:
There is no separate test day. You have 36 exercises; testing them in one session is impossible and everything after the first few would be measured under fatigue. Instead the first rotation is the test — every exercise appears within six sessions, and you train normally throughout.

Session A · the bench 1RM. You have chosen to test a true max rather than a heavy triple. That is your call and it is fine — here is how to make it count.

  • First thing in the session, fully fresh, after the full warm-up ramp.
  • Spotter physically standing there. Not nearby. This is the one session where that is non-negotiable.
  • Small jumps at the top. Empty bar → 40 → 60 → 80 → 95 → 105 → 112 → then 2.5–5 kg increments. Rest 3–5 min above 90%.
  • Stop at the first genuine grind. A missed rep is worth far less than a number 2.5 kg lower. Maximum three attempts above 95%.
  • Then do the rest of the session as written, back-offs included, at whatever the max supports.

Expect it to under-read. You have not touched heavy singles in months, so this first max is limited by skill and neural familiarity, not by muscle. It is a floor, not a ceiling — do not be discouraged if it lands below what you feel capable of. That gap closes in the first block on its own.

One adjustment for week 1 only: a true max costs three to five days of recovery, and Session E's bench volume lands later in the rotation. Run E's bench at about 5% lighter than prescribed that first week. Normal from week 2.

Session A and beyond · the RPE 10 tests. For weighted pull-ups and dips, an all-out set is safe — you fail and let go, nothing lands on you. But do not test a true single. Work up to a set of 3–6 reps taken to genuine failure instead. The estimated max from a 3–6 rep set is more reliable than one from a single, and the joint stress of a maximal weighted pull-up with a heavy belt is meaningfully higher for no extra information.

  • Session A — bench 1RM · normal-grip pull-up to failure · incline press to RPE 8
  • Session B — leg press to RPE 8
  • Session C — weighted dip to failure · bench variation. No AMRAP this rotation — it needs a settled bench number to sit against, so the app prescribes technique work instead and the first standardised AMRAP is rotation 2.
  • Session D — chin-up to failure · overhead ladder rung 1
  • Session E — bench prescribed from A (5% lighter this week) · wide-grip pulldown to failure
  • Session F — hack squat and leg curl to RPE 8

Everything else — laterals, curls, pushdowns, abs, calves. Pick a weight you think lands near the target, do the reps, log what happened. If the guess is off the app corrects it and session two prescribes properly. Guessing wrong costs nothing.

knowledge.t: The grip-width test — week 2, not week 1
knowledge.c:
Do this in Session A of week 2, once you have a settled max and are not also testing it. Testing a max and testing grips in the same session gives you two bad answers instead of one good one.

Protocol. Work up to roughly 85–88% of your new max, then:

  • One single with ring fingers on the rings (your current grip, ~73 cm). Rest 3 min.
  • One single with index fingers on the rings (~81 cm, the legal maximum). Rest 3 min.
  • One single with hands inside the rings (narrow). Rest 3 min.

Judge on bar speed and how it felt off the chest, not on whether you completed it — all three should be completable at 85%. Run a second round if two feel equal. Log the grip on every set so the answer is in the data rather than in your memory.

What to expect. At 190 cm the 81 cm competition cap does not scale with your arm length, so even your widest legal grip is functionally moderate — which makes your bench more triceps-dominant than a shorter lifter's. The theoretical case for "as wide as legal" is weakest for exactly your proportions, and reputable coaches genuinely disagree: Josh Bryant reports four of his 300 kg-plus benchers using narrow or moderate grips.

Then commit. Whichever wins becomes your competition grip and does not change again. Grip variation belongs in the variation slot — close-grip bench already covers the narrow end — not on the lift you are measuring. The entire progression depends on holding one thing steady.

knowledge.t: When a set feels easier than prescribed
knowledge.c:
This is the most-asked question and it has two different answers depending on how the set was written.

Fixed reps + an RPE target → change the load, not the reps. If you are prescribed 5 @ RPE 8 and finish 5 feeling like you had four left, do not keep going. Log it honestly as 5 reps at RPE 6, and add 2.5–5 kg on the next set. Seven reps at 100 kg is a different exercise from five at 100 kg, and once you start extending sets you can no longer compare this week's 5s to last week's 5s. The measurement system depends on holding one variable steady.

A rep range + an RIR target → change the reps, then the load. On 3×8–12 at 1–2 RIR, if you hit 8 with four in the tank, absolutely keep going. Stop where 1–2 RIR actually lands. If you reach 12 with reps still there, stop at 12 and add weight next session. That is double progression, and the range exists precisely for this.

A set marked to failure → go until failure, whatever the number. There is no prescription to violate.

One line: fixed reps means the load moves. A range means the reps move.

knowledge.t: Why not everything goes to failure — and what would change if it did
knowledge.c:
You have historically taken nearly every set to failure, so this deserves a real answer rather than a rule.

What failure genuinely buys. The relationship between proximity to failure and hypertrophy is real and in your predicted direction. Across 55 studies, growth improves as you approach failure at about 0.019 standardised units per rep in reserve. So going from 2 RIR to failure is worth roughly 0.038 SMD — about one percentage point of extra growth across a block. Real, but smaller than the measurement error in most of these studies, and smaller than what one extra set per muscle per week gives you.

What it buys for strength: nothing. Across 243 effects, the relationship between proximity to failure and 1RM has a confidence interval straddling zero. Failure does not make you stronger. It only makes you more tired.

What it costs. Muscle damage roughly 0.76 SMD higher, creatine kinase at 48 hours 0.86 higher, session RPE 1.93 higher. Concretely: a compound set to failure delays recovery 24–48 hours. Sub-failure work recovers in about six.

So if you took the bench to failure every session: you would gain about one percentage point of extra chest growth, gain nothing on your bench, and lose the ability to bench four times a week — because two of those four sessions would land inside the recovery window of the previous one. You would trade your best strength lever for your smallest hypertrophy lever.

Where failure is not optional. At light loads it is essential: at 30% of 1RM, sets to failure produced 7.8% growth versus 2.8% for sets stopped short. That is why every cable, machine and isolation exercise here ends in failure — high reps only work if you actually get there.

And the feeling is not the signal. In a study where the same 18 lifters trained one leg to failure and one leg to 2 RIR, the sub-failure leg scored better on discomfort, session RPE and mood — and grew 6.98% versus 6.96%. The sensation of insufficiency was completely uncorrelated with the outcome.

knowledge.t: Bar speed and intent
knowledge.c:
On compounds: roughly two seconds down, then accelerate as hard as you physically can. In a study that equated load and volume exactly and varied only concentric intent, maximal intent produced +18.2% on the bench and deliberately slow lifting produced +9.7%. Double the gain from identical work, with 38% less time under tension.

Two things people get wrong. Intent is not the same as speed — at 92% the bar moves slowly no matter what you do, and that is fine, because intent is about the attempt not the result. And intent is not looser form: the eccentric stays controlled, the pause stays honest, the bar path stays the same. Only the concentric changes.

Not on isolation. Explosive lateral raises become swinging, which takes tension off the exact muscle you are trying to grow. Control there.

The rule: intent when you are training force production, control when you are training a muscle. And note the intent effect disappears at failure — fatigue recruits everything regardless — so on the isolation sets that go to failure, intent is irrelevant anyway. The two rules agree.

knowledge.t: Rest periods
knowledge.c:
• Heavy singles and doubles — 3–5 min
  • Heavy back-offs, 3–5 reps — 3–4 min
  • Volume bench, 5s at 75–80% — 2.5–3 min
  • Speed bench — 90–120 s, enough to stay fast
  • Bench variations — 2.5–3 min
  • Weighted pull-ups and dips — 2–3 min
  • Incline press, rows — 2 min
  • Leg press, hack squat — 2–3 min
  • Isolation: laterals, curls, pushdowns, flies — 60–90 s
  • Jumps — full recovery, 2–3 min. Never conditioning.

Why long on compounds and short on isolation. With long rests, per-session growth for a muscle plateaus around 6–8 sets. With short rests it extends further but needs roughly double the volume to get the same result. So spend your long rests where the load actually matters, and keep isolation dense — you are chasing failure there anyway and the absolute load is not the point.

knowledge.t: Warm-up
knowledge.c:
Every session, about 5 minutes. Three to five minutes on a bike, rower or incline walk until you are genuinely warm. Then band pull-aparts 2×20, band external rotations 2×15 per side, scapular push-ups 1×10, and wrist circles with light flexion and extension.

The shoulder and elbow work is not decoration. You are pressing four times a week — this is the tissue that has to survive it.

Bench ramp on the heavy day, working toward a 105 kg top single: empty bar ×10–15, 40×5, 60×5, 80×3, 92×2, 100×1, then the work set. Rest 60–90 s on the light ramp sets and 2–3 min before the top single. The ramp is not training — never let it accumulate fatigue.

On the volume day: empty bar ×15, 50×5, 70×5, 82×3, then work sets.

Accessories: one feeder set at roughly half your working weight. That is all. There is no need to ramp a lateral raise.

knowledge.t: Where to put rest days
knowledge.c:
Both placements are legitimate, for different reasons. Resting after a hard session removes fatigue that is actually present — it peaks 24–48 hours after heavy or failure work. Resting before means you perform better on that specific day.

Which you want depends on what the session is for:

  • After A (heavy) — the fatigue is real, and going in slightly tired costs you little because the load is autoregulated by RPE anyway.
  • Before C (AMRAP) — this is a measurement, and a tired reading is a corrupted reading. Worse than a bad workout.
  • Before D or F — jumps and speed work are worthless when fatigued.
  • E — genuinely does not matter.

Simple version: rest after A, rest before C. If you only get one rest day, put it after A. Never rest between E and F — the speed day is deliberately cheap and partly exists to flush the volume day.

knowledge.t: Missing sessions — you are probably overthinking it
knowledge.c:
With a rolling rotation, a missed day is not a decision you have to make. There is no "which session do I drop." You simply do the next one in the rotation the next time you train.

  • Six sessions in seven days → a full rotation.
  • Five in seven → the rotation takes about eight days. Nothing changes. Do not compensate.
  • Four in seven, once → same. Keep going.

You only switch templates when you know in advance you will be limited for two weeks or more — Christmas, a trip, a heavy work period. Then use the 4-day or 3-day version and switch back afterward.

"Drop Session D" is different advice for a different problem: chronic under-recovery. If sleep has been under 7 hours for a week or more, D is the cheapest session to lose. That is a recovery decision, not a scheduling one.

Missing a whole week is fine. Muscle does not detrain meaningfully in seven days. Come back at the same loads.

knowledge.t: Setup, every single time
knowledge.c:
1. Eyes under the bar. Feet planted. Moderate arch — from the upper back, never the lower.
  2. Grip: ring fingers on the rings, which is roughly 73 cm and about 8 cm inside the legal maximum.
  3. Shoulder blades back and down. Not just back — down. Think about putting them in your back pockets.
  4. Unrack, then pause 2–3 seconds to re-settle the arch, re-plant the feet, re-tighten the lats. This was the best free advice you have been given and it costs nothing.
  5. Big breath, hold it.

The rep. Two seconds down to the same spot every time, just below the nipple line. Pause about a second on the chest, bar dead, still tight. Then drive with maximal intent. Bar path is a J-curve — back and up off the chest, then vertical once the bar is over the shoulder joint. Leg drive pushes the feet into the floor and toward your head, not up; nothing should lift off the bench.

knowledge.t: Your specific leaks
knowledge.c:
1 · Rushing sets. The single biggest free improvement available to you. Rushing means an inconsistent touch point, a variable bar path, and a bounce that inflates your numbers without building the strength underneath. It also means every rep is a slightly different lift, so your body never grooves one motor pattern.

2 · Long arms. At 190 cm your range of motion is long and your moment arms are long. Grip width and bar path optimisation are worth more to you than to most lifters. The 81 cm competition grip cap does not scale with arm length, so your maximum legal grip is functionally a moderate grip — which makes your bench more triceps-dominant than a shorter lifter's.

3 · The arch. Moderate is the right call given your back. Build range through thoracic extension and hip flexor mobility, never through lumbar hyperextension. A big arch is a sustained loaded lumbar extension, repeated four times a week — for you that is the wrong trade.

knowledge.t: The heavy single rules
knowledge.c:
1. Write the load range down before you start. Pre-commit. This is the whole ballgame.
  2. Maximum two singles above 90%. Then stop, regardless of how good they felt.
  3. Never miss a rep. A miss means the ceiling failed, not that you were unlucky.
  4. If you had to psych up, it was too heavy. No slaps, no ammonia, no music change. RPE 8 should feel businesslike.
  5. Back-offs are not optional.

Why 96–100% is a testing zone and not a training zone. Sheiko's system has exactly two days in a fourteen-week cycle where athletes go to 100%, and international-level athletes are capped at 90% and never touch a true max in training at all. Prilepin allots 4–10 total reps to the entire above-90% band per session. And technique measurably degrades at maximal loads — sticking-region duration increases, the bar drifts horizontally, and left-right asymmetry rises sharply. Singles at 90–94% are technique practice. Singles at 98–100% are practice at compensating.

knowledge.t: The AMRAP — how to not waste it
knowledge.c:
This is the most important 90 seconds of your week, and it is a measurement before it is a workout.

  • Same load family every time within a block. Pick something in the 80–87% window and keep it. Comparability is the entire point.
  • Same bench standard. Paused, about one second, moderate arch. A touch-and-go rep does not go in the log next to a paused one.
  • Done first, straight after the warm-up ramp. It used to sit after four sets of variation work, which corrupted it.
  • Get a spotter — physically standing there, not "nearby." No spotter means the AMRAP moves to dumbbells or a machine that day.
  • Never more than one per week. A compound set to failure costs 24–48 hours. Two per week and each reading is taken against incomplete recovery from the last, which makes the whole series meaningless.

Why 80–87% and not something lighter. At that range the rep count agrees between sessions to within about one rep and the estimated-max formula error is near its minimum. At 70%, the between-person spread runs from 6 to 28 reps and the error roughly doubles. A moderate-rep AMRAP feels productive and tells you almost nothing.

knowledge.t: Working max vs observed e1RM
knowledge.c:
Two different numbers, and confusing them is how people overreach without noticing.

Observed e1RM is computed from every qualifying set. It is a continuous record and it is never overwritten.

Working max is what prescriptions are calculated from, and it updates only at block boundaries.

Why not update it every time you have a good day. Test–retest variability on a 1RM in trained lifters is about 3.3%, which on a 130 kg bench is ±4 kg of pure noise. If the working max ratchets up on every good session, six weeks later you are training at a genuine RPE 9.5 while believing you are at 8. That is overreaching by arithmetic, and it is almost impossible to detect from the inside.

The rule: at block end, set the working max to the best observed e1RM from that block's index sets. Bump early only if observed exceeds working by more than 5% for two consecutive weeks. Never lower it mid-block — a bad week is a bad week, not a strength loss.

knowledge.t: Index sets — why only some sets count
knowledge.c:
One designated set per key lift, done fresh, once per rotation. Those are the sets the estimated max is read from.

  • Comp bench — the AMRAP in Session C (to failure), plus the top single in Session A as a second reading
  • All three pull-up grips — tracked as three separate exercises with three separate maxes. Wide will sit 10–15% below normal grip and chin-ups above it; that is expected. Never compare them to each other.
  • Incline press — first working set, Session C
  • Weighted pull-up — first working set, Session A
  • Weighted dip — first working set, Session E
  • Leg press — first working set, Session B

A top set at a known RPE gives a cleaner estimated max than a set to failure, at a fraction of the fatigue cost. Only the bench AMRAP needs to go to failure, because it is the one number we want zero interpretation on.

Why not a weekly failure set on everything. It would reintroduce exactly the fatigue problem the plan is designed around — and for isolation exercises an estimated max is not meaningful anyway. One validation study found all nine standard prediction equations failed on the arm curl.

knowledge.t: What good actually looks like
knowledge.c:
Weight up, waist flat, lifts up. That is the whole target state. If you see it, change nothing.

  • Gaining under 0.1 kg/week → add roughly 250 kcal, realistically one extra meal-sized snack.
  • Gaining over 0.6 kg/week → cut roughly 300 kcal.
  • Waist rising nearly as fast as bodyweight → slow the bulk regardless of what the scale says.
  • e1RM flat for four weeks while bodyweight rises → that is a recovery or programming problem, not a food problem. Send me the export.

Adjust on 2–3 week trends, never on single readings. Individual days are noise. Only the 7-day average means anything.

knowledge.t: Targets
knowledge.c:
• Weeks 1–12: +0.4–0.5 kg per week. You are regaining tissue you already had, and muscle memory means this window converts food into muscle at a far better ratio than the rest of the bulk will. Push while it is true.
  • Weeks 13–33: +0.2–0.25 kg per week. Throttle back once you are past your old peak.
  • Protein 1.6–2.2 g/kg — roughly 150–200 g/day.
  • Creatine monohydrate 3–5 g/day. Any time, no loading phase. The best-evidenced supplement that exists and the one obvious gap in your current stack.

knowledge.t: Steering without counting calories
knowledge.c:
You need two instruments and one rule.

Scale — every morning, after the toilet, before food. Only the 7-day average counts. Tape measure — waist at the navel, once a week, relaxed, same time of day.

The rule: adjust on 2–3 week trends, never on single readings.

The one thing worth actually counting is protein, and only for two weeks. Everything else can be eyeballed on a bulk because the scale tells you whether total intake is right. Protein is the only nutrient where you cannot see the deficit until months of training have been wasted. Count it until you know what 180 g looks like on your plate, then stop.

A trick for untracked meals. Do not try to estimate them. Instead make sure your tracked portions — breakfast, post-workout, before bed — reliably deliver 120–140 g of protein. Then whatever the untracked meals add is a bonus rather than a gap.

Your anchors: Greek yoghurt, chicken, eggs, milk, quark, whey, lean beef, fish. Carbs: rice, potatoes, oats, bread, pasta, bananas. Fats: olive oil, nuts, whole eggs, fatty fish. You have picked well already.

knowledge.t: Carbs — when it actually matters
knowledge.c:
Honestly, on a surplus with a big appetite you will be well-fuelled almost all the time and this barely matters. Where it does:

  • Before A and E — a carb-based meal 2–3 hours prior. These are the two sessions where being under-fuelled visibly costs performance, and E is a measurement, so a flat day corrupts data rather than just a workout.
  • Before C — same. Highest total work of the rotation.
  • Before D and F — does not matter much. Train fasted if you prefer.
  • During a deload — do not cut food. The deload is for recovering, and recovery costs energy.

If a session feels flat and it is not sleep, it is almost always carbs from the day before rather than that morning. Glycogen refills over about 24 hours.

Do not do anything clever. No carb cycling, no timing protocols, no fasting windows. On a bulk with your appetite, "eat enough and eat protein" captures 95% of the available benefit.

knowledge.t: Steps, basketball and where to put them
knowledge.c:
Keep the walking. It burns energy without meaningfully interfering with lifting, lets you eat more without gaining fat as fast, and aids recovery. Treat step count as a dial — if the waist is creeping, add steps before you cut food.

Basketball placement:

  • On a rest day — best
  • After Session B or F, legs already done — fine
  • The day before F — fine, but skip the jumps that session
  • The day before or of the AMRAP — avoid, it corrupts the measurement

The one real conflict: basketball involves a lot of jumping and hard landings. If you have played, drop the jump work from Session F that cycle. You already got the stimulus, and doubling up is how the back gets aggravated.

If your back is sore after basketball, log it. That tells us something about what actually provokes it, which is more than you currently know.

knowledge.t: Deloads
knowledge.c:
Earned, not scheduled. There is no fixed deload week. Rotation 15 is a planned Recovery rotation, and beyond that the app offers a deload when two of your own triggers fire together — the readings it is already watching.

Taking one: keep all six sessions, cut volume 40–50%, drop top-end intensity about 10%, everything at 3+ RIR minimum.

Never take a full rest week. A controlled trial found complete cessation actually impaired strength relative to training through, and the cessation group reported more soreness and less motivation — the opposite of the intended effect.

The triggers are your top single dropping more than 5% below your recent average at the same RPE for two sessions, sleep under 7 hours for a week, or two niggles inside one block. Two of them together is the signal; one on its own is not.

knowledge.t: When things go wrong
knowledge.c:
• Top single 5%+ below average, twice → one deload trigger. Two together and the app offers one
  • Sleep under 7 h for a week → drop Session D, the cheapest to lose
  • Two or more niggles in a block → rotate the aggravating variation out, do not push through
  • Lower back flares → cut leg press range, drop jumps, keep reverse hypers, keep everything upper. Log what provoked it.
  • Shoulder aches on the overhead ladder → drop a rung immediately
  • Missed the AMRAP → move it to the next session. Never do two in one week to catch up.
  • e1RM flat 4 weeks while bodyweight rises → send the export. Recovery or programming, not food.
  • Sick or genuinely wrecked → skip. Resume at the next session. Nothing is lost.
  • Missed a whole week → come back at the same loads.

knowledge.t: What we are aiming at, honestly
knowledge.c:
Peaked 140 kg by end of March70–80% likely
Normal-day 140 kg by end of March40–50%
150 kg in any form by Marchunlikely

The most probable outcome is a normal-day bench around 130–135 with a peaked max of 140–145, at roughly 95–98 kg bodyweight, with visibly bigger delts, arms and upper chest.

The thing that actually decides it is not in this app. Your history is short bursts of progress separated by long plateaus in a deficit — which means you have never once run a structured programme in a sustained surplus. That is not a small missing variable. It is the whole thing.

Finishing 33 weeks of this matters more than any single decision inside it.

knowledge.t: Myo-reps — how to actually do them
knowledge.c:
One activation set taken to genuine failure at 12–20 reps. Rack it, breathe for 15–20 seconds, then do 3–5 mini-sets of 3–5 reps with 15–20 seconds between them. Stop when you can no longer get three clean reps. The whole thing takes about two minutes.

Why it works. The activation set does the hard part — it fatigues the muscle enough that every subsequent rep recruits the high-threshold fibres immediately. The mini-sets are then almost pure effective reps, with none of the warm-up cost of a fresh straight set. A trial comparing myo-reps against traditional straight sets found the same size and strength gains with roughly 30% less total volume load, in about 60% less time.

What that means for you. The finding is about efficiency, not superiority. So they are added to the end of an exercise here rather than replacing sets — you are not short of time, you are chasing stimulus. Three exercises carry them: overhead triceps extension in A, EZ curl in E, lateral raise in F.

Where they do not belong. Anything heavy, anything barbell, anything where failure has a cost. Never on the bench.

knowledge.t: Static holds and why they are gated to block 2
knowledge.c:
2–3 holds of 5–10 seconds at 105–115% of your current max. Rack pins set, spotter present, always. Unrack, hold at lockout, re-rack. You never lower the bar.

What they do. Three things: they desensitise you to loads above your max, so competition weight stops feeling heavy; they build lockout strength and connective-tissue tolerance; and they can potentiate the sets that follow.

What they do not do. They are joint-angle specific — a lockout hold trains your lockout. At 190 cm with long arms your sticking point is almost certainly mid-range, so these are a confidence and load-exposure tool, not a fix for your weak point. That is what the pin press in the variation slot is for.

Why not before block 2. You are coming off a cut. Hanging 115% of your max on your elbows before the connective tissue has re-adapted is how you buy a six-week layoff. The app will not show them until block 2 — that is deliberate, not an oversight.

knowledge.t: Why there are two heavy singles a week now
knowledge.c:
Session A takes a top single at the block's RPE cap. Session C now opens with a primer single one full RPE point lighter, before the 5×5.

Why this is nearly free. Heavy pressing singles are not very fatiguing — far less than heavy squats or pulls. The cost of a single is skill and connective tissue, not systemic recovery. Frequency is also the single strongest predictor of strength gain there is: each added bench day up to about four is worth roughly 28% faster progress, even with volume matched.

Why the primer is lighter. At RPE 7.5 it is practice, not a test. It also potentiates the volume work that follows, so the 5×5 tends to feel better, not worse. The Eastern-bloc programmes that produced the best bench pressers in history are built almost entirely on submaximal frequency: build and practise, do not test.

The rule that still holds. Maximum two singles above 90% in a session, and never miss a rep. In blocks 4 and 5 session A takes two; everywhere else it takes one.

knowledge.t: Do weighted pull-ups build your bench?
knowledge.c:
Partly, and for reasons that are not the ones usually given.

What is true. A bench press is a closed chain against the bench, so the upper back is the surface you press from — a bigger, tighter one puts more force into the bar and less into you sinking. A thicker back also raises your chest, which shortens the bar path for free. And the lats own the “back” half of the J-shaped bar path and control the descent: a bench where the bar drifts and the shoulders lose position is usually a lat problem, not a pec problem. Pulling volume is also most of what keeps your shoulders willing to keep benching.

What is not. The lats do not push the bar up. And the usual evidence — strong-pull-up people have strong benches — is badly confounded: they train hard, have trained for years, and are not fat. Those predict a strong bench on their own.

So: a weighted pull-up is the best back exercise you can progressively load, and back size is worth building on a bulk for its own sake. Treat it as that, and you will not be disappointed on the week your pull-up moves and your bench does not. The plan already gives you A5 (pull-up, 4 × 5–8), D5 (chin-up, 3 × 6–10) and rows at A6, C5, E5 and F3. This is already well covered.

knowledge.t: Pauses, dead stops and the Spoto press
knowledge.c:
This one is straightforwardly true, and it is the more useful of the two things people tell you.

A touch-and-go bench borrows from three things at the bottom: the stretch reflex storing elastic energy in the eccentric, the rib cage bouncing the bar, and — if you are honest — momentum. A pause removes all three, which does two things. It trains the position where you are actually weak, since almost everyone’s hardest inch is just off the chest and touch-and-go is the one style that lets you skip past it. And it removes the place where technique hides: if your bar path or shoulder position is wrong, a pause makes you hold that wrong position under load and find out.

  • Paused bench — touch, hold motionless 1–2 s, press. The default, for everyone.
  • Spoto press — stop 2–3 cm above the chest and hold. No contact, no rest, relentless. Excellent for control.
  • Pin press / dead stop — the bar sits dead on pins near chest height and you press from zero. The purest off-the-chest strength, with no elastic contribution at all.

Your plan already agrees. C2 is exactly this — the bench variation, 3 × 4–6 at RPE 8, with its own tracked working max. A1’s static hold against the pins is a close cousin. If you want a recommendation for which of the three to run: Spoto while the loads are moderate, pin press in the heavier blocks.

Two cautions. A pause is not a rest — the tension never leaves, you are just not moving. And on pin presses, stay tight under the bar between reps; relaxing completely under a loaded bar at chest height is how shoulders get hurt.

knowledge.t: Where the bar stalls, and what that means
knowledge.c:
Where the bar slows down tells you what to train. Watch a set from the side, or just feel it.

  • Off the chest — the pecs at long length, plus position lost at the bottom. Train it with pauses, Spoto and pin presses, a slightly wider grip, and incline work.
  • Mid-range — pec and front delt strength. Train it with close-grip bench, volume fives and dips.
  • Lockout — the triceps, almost always. Train it with close-grip, high pin or board presses, and overhead extensions. This is the most common stall and the most fixable.

Worth knowing about your own plan: in a typical rotation it gives the long head of the triceps about 9.0 sets a week against 20.5 for the lateral and medial heads. The long head crosses the shoulder, so it is only loaded at long length when the arm is overhead — pushdowns, skullcrushers and close-grip work all train the other two heads far more. Every long-head set you get comes from A8 and E7. If one thing were ever added to the pressing side of this plan, a second overhead extension slot is the one to argue for.

And the two things nobody trains: external rotation for the rotator cuff (two light sets, twice a week — ten minutes a month against the injury most likely to end a bench cycle), and the serratus anterior, which is what holds the shoulder blade against the rib cage and therefore what “tight upper back” actually depends on. Neither appears anywhere in this app’s muscle model, so the volume analytics cannot warn you about them.

knowledge.t: What actually moves a bench, in order
knowledge.c:
The arguing usually goes wrong because people compare exercises when the first three items are not exercises.

1 · Bodyweight. On a bulk this is the cheapest bench progress available and it is not cheating: more mass means a thicker torso, a shorter bar path and more leverage into the bench. The rough rule of thumb is half to one kilo on the bench per kilo of bodyweight, early in a gaining phase.

2 · Frequency and specificity. This plan benches in four sessions of six with four different jobs — heavy singles and triples, an AMRAP, volume fives, speed work. Nothing on this list beats benching more skilfully more often.

3 · Technique. Every one of these is worth more than any accessory: set the shoulder blades back and down and keep them there for the whole set, including the unrack; arch what you have and drive the floor away horizontally rather than lifting the hips; remember the bar path is a J, not a line; keep the elbows around 45–75° from the torso; try to snap the bar apart, which switches the whole shoulder girdle on for free; control the eccentric and then be violent, on every rep including warm-ups.

4 · Then, and only then, the accessories. Close-grip bench is the single best assistance exercise — same groove, more triceps, most direct transfer. Weighted dips are the best bench-shaped hypertrophy exercise and load easily (C3). Overhead triceps extension is the most under-trained muscle in most benches. Incline press covers the upper chest at a different angle (A4, E3/E4). Overhead press builds lockout stability (F2). Rows and pull-ups build the platform. Rear delts and face pulls add no kilos at all — they keep you healthy enough to keep adding them, which over 33 rotations is the same thing.

knowledge.t: Cheap tricks that buy real stimulus
knowledge.c:
The speed day is one of these — maximal intent at 60–70% recruits high-threshold fibres without the fatigue of a heavy set, and volume-equated it was worth +18.2% on the bench against +9.7% for deliberately slow lifting. Here are the others this plan uses, all on the same principle: buy stimulus without buying fatigue.

  • Lengthened-position emphasis. Flies with the arms travelling behind the torso, incline curls with the elbows behind you, overhead extensions with a full stretch. Training a muscle at long lengths produces meaningfully more growth than training it short, and it costs nothing but attention.
  • A pause in the stretch. One to two seconds at the bottom of a fly or a curl. Free, and it removes the bounce that was doing part of the work.
  • Myo-reps. Two minutes for roughly the stimulus of three straight sets, on movements where failure is free.
  • The primer single. A heavy single before volume work potentiates the sets that follow.
  • Failure aimed, not cut. Every row, face pull and isolation set finishes at or near failure. Every heavy press stops short. Proximity to failure drives hypertrophy and has essentially no relationship with strength gain — so this costs your bench nothing and buys size everywhere else.

The common thread: fatigue is the currency. Anything that raises stimulus without spending it is worth taking.

knowledge.t: Deloads are earned, not scheduled
knowledge.c:
This plan has no scheduled deload, and that is a deliberate change from how most programmes are written.

Why. The evidence is thinner than the folklore. A controlled trial that placed a one-week deload at the midpoint of a programme found it slightly reduced lower-body strength gains against training straight through, with no hypertrophy benefit either way. Another found complete cessation actively impaired strength, with more soreness and less motivation, not less. The risk of genuine non-functional overreaching without deloading is low.

What replaces it. The app watches the triggers this plan already names — a top set more than 5% below your rolling average, sleep under 7 hours, two or more niggles in a block — and offers a deload when two of them fire together. One trigger is a bad week. Two is a pattern.

What a deload looks like when you take one. Keep all six sessions. Cut volume about 45%, drop everything to RPE 7, nothing to failure, for one rotation. You are not resting; you are training lightly. That distinction is the whole point.

knowledge.t: What the tape measure tells you that the scale cannot
knowledge.c:
The scale tells you whether you are gaining. It cannot tell you what you are gaining. That is what the tape is for, and it matters just as much on a cut as on a bulk.

On a bulk, you want arms, chest and shoulders climbing faster than the waist. If the waist is rising at more than roughly a third of the rate bodyweight is, the surplus is too big — slow it down regardless of what the scale says.

On a cut, you want the opposite: waist falling fast while the arms and chest hold. If the arms are falling as fast as the waist, you are losing muscle and the deficit is too aggressive.

How to take them. Same time of day, relaxed, no flexing, waist at the navel. Consistency of method beats precision — a slightly wrong number taken the same way every week is far more useful than an accurate one taken differently each time.

The Progress screen shows every site with its rate of change per week, next to what bodyweight did over the same stretch. That comparison is the entire point of measuring.

knowledge.t: How much volume is enough
knowledge.c:
The honest answer from the current evidence: more sets keep producing more growth, with diminishing returns and no clear ceiling that anyone has managed to identify. The largest meta-regression to date — 67 studies, over 2,000 subjects — found hypertrophy still climbing at the top of the range studied. Strength, by contrast, shows much sharper diminishing returns: you do not need much volume to get strong, you need frequency and practice.

What limits you is not the stimulus. It is recovery, session length, and joints. That is why this plan puts its volume where it is cheap — cables, machines, isolation — and keeps it lean where it is expensive.

Per session, returns become hard to detect past roughly 11 fractional sets for one muscle in one workout. No session here exceeds that, which is why the work is spread across four to five exposures a week rather than piled into two.

On counting. A set counts fractionally: 1.0 where the muscle is the main mover, 0.5 for a meaningful supporting role, nothing below 0.3. That fractional method predicts growth better than counting direct sets alone. The whole-muscle figures on the Plan screen take the largest head contribution per set rather than adding heads together — adding them double counts, and the familiar ~20-sets-a-week figure is a whole-muscle number.

knowledge.t: Where the estimated max comes from
knowledge.c:
A one-rep max is a number you almost never want to measure. Testing it costs a session, adds fatigue you then have to recover from, and buys one data point about that day — that sleep, that mood, that room temperature.

So the app estimates it instead, from every set you log. That estimate is e1RM, and it works because of one reliable fact: how many reps you can do with a load is a stable function of what fraction of your max that load is. Five reps and no more means roughly 86%. Turn that around and you have a max you never tested.

Percentage of your one-rep max you can lift for n reps to failure — the app’s own table.

Read the shape. The first reps are the expensive ones: going from a single to a triple costs nearly 8% of your max, while going from eight reps to ten costs under 5%. That curvature is exactly why “3 × 3” and “3 × 3 at 86%” stop being the same instruction on a bad day.

knowledge.t: What one point of RPE is worth
knowledge.c:
Reps alone are not enough. A set of five that nearly killed you and a set of five you strolled through are not the same evidence, and what separates them is the effort rating.

RPE 10 means no more reps were available. RPE 9 means one more. RPE 8 means two. Once the app has reps and RPE it knows how many reps the load was really worth, and it can read the curve. A set logged without an effort rating gets no estimate rather than a guessed one — that is deliberate.

The same curve, once per RPE. Darker is closer to failure.

The curves are near-parallel, which is the useful property: a point of RPE is worth about the same percentage wherever you are in the rep range. At five reps, RPE 8 → RPE 9 is 81.1% → 83.7%. That is 2.6% of your max — roughly 3 kg on a 115 kg bench.

So a set you rate one point too hard drags your estimate down about 3 kg, and one rated too easy inflates it by the same. Rate honestly, and rate it before you rack the bar — the question is how many more could I have done at that bar speed, not how much did that hurt.

knowledge.t: Why this app uses a table, not a formula
knowledge.c:
There is no single equation everyone agrees on, and the disagreement is not small. The classic ones were each fitted to a different population doing a different lift.

  • Epley (1985) — 1RM = w × (1 + reps/30). The most widely used. Linear in reps, so it grows steadily more optimistic at the top end.
  • Brzycki (1993) — 1RM = w × 36/(37 − reps). Tracks Epley to about ten reps, then falls away. It divides by zero at 37 reps, which tells you how far it was meant to be pushed.
  • Lombardi (1989) — 1RM = w × reps^0.10. A power law, and much the most conservative at high reps.
  • Wathen (1994) — an exponential decay with a floor, which describes the physiology better than a straight line: the curve flattens rather than falling forever.

Four methods on a set taken to failure. They agree to about six reps and then fan out.

On a 100 kg set the four are within about 5 kg of each other up to five reps. At ten reps they span 8.9 kg. At twelve reps they span 15.8 kg — a sixth of the lift.

What this app uses is not a formula but the RPE table from Tuchscherer’s Reactive Training Systems, refined in Helms’ work on autoregulation. It is empirical: it encodes what strength athletes actually do. Its real advantage is the second axis — every formula above needs a set taken to failure to mean anything, and will quietly return a far-too-low number if you feed it a set with three reps left.

And it stops at twelve. Past that the spread above is only the disagreement between formulas; the disagreement between lifters is larger still, because rep performance at 70% depends on fibre type and conditioning rather than on maximal strength. The app returns nothing rather than something confident and wrong.

knowledge.t: Why 7 reps and 6 reps give the same number
knowledge.c:
The table has rows for 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 10 and 12 reps. It has no row for 7, 9 or 11. The app snaps a set to the nearest row and ties go down, which is the conservative direction — the lower row prescribes the lighter load.

Estimated max from a 100 kg set at RPE 10. The orange bars are reps with no row of their own.

So six reps at 95 kg and seven reps at 95 kg both estimate 113.5 kg. That is not a bug; it is the table being honest that it has no data for seven. But it does mean that on an AMRAP, going from six to seven will not move your number, and going from seven to eight will move it by nearly 8 kg at once. Do not read the flat step as a stalled block.

Two other things worth knowing about the estimate:

  • It is exercise-specific. The load–rep relationship differs between lifts — a lifter who gets five reps at 86% on the bench may get eight at 86% on a leg press. That is why the plan tracks separate working maxes for the competition bench, the variation, incline dumbbell, incline Smith, dips, pull-ups and the leg press instead of scaling one number.
  • A single set is a sample, not a max. True maximal strength moves several percent day to day. A trend across sessions is worth far more than the best number in it, which is why every figure comes with a confidence and a sample count.
